Top Tips for Endoscopic Management of Lynch Syndrome and Familial Adenomatous Polyposis
  • Source: Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (2026)
  • Topic: Endoscopic surveillance and management strategies for Lynch syndrome and FAP
  • Author(s): Bryson W. Katona, MD, PhD (University of Pennsylvania)
1. Lynch Syndrome Surveillance Intervals
  • Genotype-dependent: intervals vary by gene mutation
1.1 High-Risk Genotypes (MLH1, MSH2, EPCAM)
  • Lifetime CRC risk: 50-60%
  • Start colonoscopy at age 20-25 (or 2-5 years before youngest family CRC)
  • Age <40 --> repeat every 2 years
  • Age ≥40 --> repeat every 1 year
  • If LS diagnosed age 20-24 --> offer baseline colonoscopy at diagnosis
1.2 Lower-Risk Genotypes (MSH6, PMS2)
  • MSH6: lifetime CRC risk up to 40%
  • PMS2: lifetime CRC risk up to 20%
  • Start colonoscopy at age 30-35
  • MSH6 --> repeat every 1-3 years (most safely every 2 years)
  • PMS2 --> repeat every 2-3 years
2. High-Risk Surveillance Approach for Lynch Syndrome
  • Each colonoscopy --> treat as high-risk procedure
  • No LS-specific quality metrics exist (no adenoma detection rate standard)
  • Data shows no advantage from:
  • Chromoendoscopy
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Other supplemental imaging techniques
  • Endoscopies --> performed by expert endoscopists with LS experience
  • Extra time needed for right colon (increased right-sided CRC risk in LS)
  • Consider second forward-viewing look
  • Inspection in retroflexion
  • Use of virtual chromoendoscopy
  • Overall withdrawal time --> longer than average-risk screening exams
3. Colonoscopy Cannot Prevent All Lynch Syndrome CRCs
  • Colorectal carcinogenesis can progress quickly (especially MLH1, MSH2, EPCAM)
  • Some LS-associated CRCs develop directly from MMR-deficient crypts (bypass polyp precursor)
  • Interval CRCs do occur during routine surveillance
  • Overwhelmingly identified at early stage (I or II)
  • Surgical removal --> curative
  • Colonoscopy substantially improves survival from LS-associated CRC
  • Colonoscopy remains one of the most important procedures for LS patients
4. Upper Endoscopic Surveillance in Lynch Syndrome
  • Perform regularly in all LS individuals
  • Coordinate with colonoscopy to minimize:
  • Time burden
  • Cost burden
  • Separate anesthesia exposure
  • Upper endoscopy interval may differ from colonoscopy intervals
4.1 Recommended Intervals by Genotype
  • MLH1, MSH2, EPCAM: every 2-3 years starting at age 30-35
  • MSH6: every 2 years starting at age 30-35
  • PMS2: every 2-3 years starting at age 30-35
  • NCCN guidelines do not explicitly recommend for PMS2, but opportunistic upper endoscopy should be considered
4.2 Technical Considerations
  • Visualize to third portion of duodenum
  • If duodenal neoplasia identified --> consider push enteroscopy for complete visualization
5. Gastric Biopsies in Lynch Syndrome
  • Current NCCN guidelines: perform biopsies on upper endoscopies in LS
  • Target areas:
  • Gastric body (greater and lesser curvature --> same specimen cup)
  • Antrum (greater curvature, lesser curvature, incisura --> same specimen cup)
5.1 What to Rule Out
  • Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori)
  • Gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM)
  • Autoimmune gastritis
5.2 Evidence
  • Rates of H. pylori and GIM in LS --> similar or lower than average-risk population
  • Recent data: repeating non-targeted biopsies on subsequent exams led to incremental yield in GIM detection
  • Reasonable approach: non-targeted biopsies of body and antrum on each upper endoscopic exam
6. Polyp Removal: Lynch Syndrome vs FAP
  • Lynch syndrome: complete removal of all polyps necessary
  • Exception: fundic gland polyps (FGPs) and small hyperplastic rectosigmoid polyps
  • Applies to upper GI and colorectal polyps
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): complete polyp clearance typically not possible
  • Classical FAP: hundreds to thousands of polyps present
  • Remove polyps with higher-risk features preferentially
7. Ampulla Examination
  • FAP: dedicated ampulla examination is a necessity
  • LS: not routinely recommended
7.1 FAP Ampulla Visualization Techniques
  • Use clear cap on standard forward-viewing scope (Figure 1)
  • OR use dedicated side-viewing endoscope
  • Forward-viewing scope with clear cap --> adequate visualization in ≥95% of cases
  • This method --> preferred by many expert FAP endoscopists
7.2 When to Biopsy Ampulla
  • Normal appearing ampullas in FAP: no need to biopsy (most will show adenoma if biopsied)
  • Strongly consider biopsy if ampulla appears abnormal
8. Gastric Findings in FAP
  • Fundic gland polyposis (FGPs): very common in proximal stomach
8.1 Fundic Gland Polyps
  • FGPs in FAP often display low-grade dysplasia (LGD)
  • LGD detection in FGPs --> does not meaningfully alter FAP surveillance recommendations
8.2 Antral Polyps
  • All gastric polyps in the antrum --> remove (regardless of size)
8.3 High-Risk Proximal Gastric Findings
  • White mucosal patches (Figure 1)
  • May harbor adenomatous tissue
  • If adenoma present --> resect by endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or ESD
  • Polypoid mounds in proximal stomach (Figure 1)
  • May harbor underlying dysplasia or high-risk lesions
  • Perform large area snare polypectomy to sample for assessment
9. Pouchoscopy in FAP
  • Performed after total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (TPC-IPAA)
  • Common procedure for classical FAP
9.1 Examination Requirements
  • Carefully examine entire pouch and pre-pouch ileum
  • Extra attention to rectal cuff (even if very short ~1-2cm)
  • Rectal cuff = native colorectal tissue --> high adenoma risk
9.2 Management
  • Adenomas frequently develop in cuff (Figure 1)
  • Remove adenomas endoscopically
10. Colectomy Timing in FAP
  • FAP spectrum varies widely --> decision must be individualized
10.1 Factors Favoring Early Colectomy
  • Polyps ≥10mm
  • Villous histology present
  • High-grade dysplasia present
10.2 Classical FAP Examples
  • APC codon 1309 PGVs (β-catenin binding domain)
  • Can have thousands of polyps by second decade

--> Early colectomy often necessary

10.3 Attenuated FAP
  • Typically from PGVs impacting 5' or 3' end of APC gene
  • Polyp burden may be minimal
  • Can often be managed endoscopically throughout lifetime
  • May avoid colectomy entirely
10.4 Decision-Making Process
  • Multidisciplinary approach required
  • Consider patient's personal preferences
  • Timing --> individualized based on polyp burden and risk features
11. Key Differences: Lynch Syndrome vs FAP Management
  • Colonoscopy intervals: LS genotype-dependent; FAP individualized
  • Polyp removal: complete in LS; preferential in FAP
  • Ampulla exam: not needed in LS; essential in FAP
  • Upper endoscopy: both require, but different targets and intervals
12. Summary Table: Lynch Syndrome Surveillance
Gene Upper Endoscopy Start Upper Interval Colonoscopy Start Colonoscopy Interval
MLH1, MSH2, EPCAM 30-35* 2-3 years 20-25# <40: 2 years; ≥40: 1 year
MSH6 30-35% 2 years 30-35 1-3 years
PMS2 30-35% 2-3 years 30-35 2-3 years
  • *Consider initiation prior to age 30 if family history of upper GI cancer <age 35
  • #Consider initiation 2-5 years prior to earliest CRC if diagnosed before age 25
  • %Consider initiation 2-5 years prior to earliest CRC if diagnosed before age 35
